outcomes.original: Filing step: If Planning confirms a new CUA is required, file a Conditional Use Authorization application with San Francisco Planning (fee approximately $3,100 for a no-construction CUA, CPI-adjusted). What to say: Describe the concept as a 404 sq ft full-service restaurant with full commercial kitchen, no alcohol service, five employees, operating before midnight. Emphasize that the concept serves food as the primary use with no bar, no hard liquor, and no entertainment, so it falls outside the most restrictive Mission Alcohol SUD controls. Commit to closing hours (e.g., 10 pm weekdays, 11 pm or midnight weekends), a noise and odor control plan, a good neighbor policy with a complaint log and contact number, and compliance with FOG and fire safety requirements. Submit a floor plan showing the kitchen layout, seating area, and restroom. Schedule the pre-application community meeting at least 30 days before filing, and prepare for a 30-day neighborhood notification (Planning Code §311) and a Planning Commission hearing 120-180 days after filing.
outcomes.note: The records name the zoning district and overlay but state the actual controls and procedures are in rule lines not provided; the building permit catalog does not cover CUA fees or timelines.

outcomes.original: Filing step: File for a San Francisco Business Registration Certificate with the Office of the Treasurer & Tax Collector immediately after forming the legal entity. What to say: Register online with the EIN and legal entity name; pay the tiered fee ($55 up to $100k gross receipts, $95 up to $250k, plus $4 state fee). Every other city department asks for the Business Account Number (BAN), so obtain this before filing the building permit or health applications.

outcomes.original: Filing step: Engage an architect to prepare building permit plans for the tenant improvements, kitchen build-out, and any change of occupancy, and submit the DPH plan check application concurrently with the building permit. What to say: Hire an architect who has done San Francisco restaurant projects. The plans must show the kitchen layout (hood, cooking line, sinks, storage), seating area, restroom, and ADA compliance. Submit scaled drawings, equipment cut sheets, and a menu to DPH for plan check (fee $828-$2,207 depending on project scope). File the building permit application with DBI, routing it to Planning for zoning review (Planning Code §175) and to SFFD for hood and fire safety review. State on the DBI application that Planning approval (CUA) is pending and that the building permit is contingent on that entitlement. Schedule a DPH pre-final inspection at ~80% construction completion and a final inspection before opening.

outcomes.original: Filing step: Apply for the Health Permit to Operate at least one month before the planned opening, after DPH plan check is approved. What to say: Submit the application online with the BAN, Location ID (LIN), and federal tax ID. Confirm that at least one owner or employee has completed a Certified Food Protection Manager course (ServSafe or equivalent, $100-$250, valid 5 years). Schedule the pre-opening inspection with the DPH plan reviewer at least two weeks in advance. The inspector will confirm the facility matches the approved plans, all equipment is installed, sinks have hot water, and surfaces are sealed. The permit ($470 application fee, $0 annual license fee for 2026-28) is issued after the final inspection passes.

outcomes.original: Filing step: Obtain ASCAP and BMI public performance licenses before opening if the restaurant plays recorded music (background music, streaming services). What to say: Federal copyright law requires a blanket license to play music publicly. Sign up online with ASCAP and BMI (each $300-$2,500 per year, formula-based on occupancy and music use). The licenses are effective immediately and take under a week to set up.

outcomes.original: Estimated time: 120 to 300 days. Estimated government cost: $5,500 to $21,000. Notes: The timeline is 120-300 days and the cost is $5,500-$21,000 for the entitlement path (Conditional Use Authorization, Health permit to operate, Building permit with change of use) when those approvals are granted. The range covers: CUA application and hearing (120-180 days, $3,100 fee), building permit review and issuance (14-120 days, $800-$15,000 depending on construction valuation), DPH plan check (21-60 days, $828-$2,207), and health permit to operate (14-45 days, $470 application fee). The timeline runs from CUA filing to final health permit issuance; it does not include time spent before filing (pre-application meetings, architect's design, or the Letter of Determination request). If Planning determines a new CUA is not required and the concept can proceed as an administrative change of use, the timeline and cost would drop to approximately 60-150 days and $2,500-$8,000 (building permit, DPH plan check, and health permit only). The cost does not include state business formation, architect and engineering fees, construction costs, grease interceptor installation, or insurance. Add 30-60 days to the timeline for pre-application community meetings and plan preparation before the CUA filing. The CUA is the critical path: 6-10 months including environmental review, neighborhood notification, and Planning Commission hearing scheduling. File the CUA application before or in parallel with lease negotiations, with a lease contingency clause.
